newsitem.title: FINLAND: ANALYSTS SEEK HANDSET STRENGTH IN NOKIA'S Q3. [CORRECTED 08:42 GMT]
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SEEK HANDSET STRENGTH IN NOKIA'S Q3. [CORRECTED 08:42 GMT]

text.p: Analysts want to see business as
usual and no more logistics problems in mobile phones in Finnish
telecommunications major Nokia Oy's third quarter interim report (corrects from third tertial interim report) due for release on Thursday.
Forecasts and Nokia's share price have been encouraged by
Swedish Ericsson's signals of strong markets, and as
U.S. rival Motorola has lost market share, quesses are
that Nokia has improved its position while terminating the
logistics and cost problems that dragged its mobile phones unit
to a Q1 loss.
"If Nokia comes out with a result in line with expectations,
that would indicate that earnings have improved quickly and that
there is reason to expect good results also next year, said Jari
Vayrynen, analyst at Protos Securities.
An in-line report may be enough to justify the current share
price despite an over 50 percent gain in a virtually straight
line since late July to 230.00 markka on Tuesday, analysts said.
The median of analysts' forecasts for Nokia's third quarter
profit before tax and minorities is just over one billion
markka, up from a 959 million proforma figure for last year and
well above the 728 million in the second quarter.
The mobile phones division in the second quarter reversed a
slight loss in the first to a slight profit while the
telecommunications operation remained healthy.
Nokia does not publish interim profits by division, only net
sales, which means that analysts will be reading the text
sections of the nine-month results statement particularly
diligently to get a picture of the speed of the recovery.
"I expect continued improvement in mobile phones in Q3 ...
but the most important quarter is the fourth," said Gunnar
Andersson, telecommunications analyst at Handelsbanken.
Analysts expect Nokia to have benefitted from new products,
particularly the 8110 handset launched in June, though the full
impact would not be seen until Christmas sales, which normally
make the final quarter the strongest for handsets.
Nokia CEO Jorma Ollila said in August that the 8110 product
had got a "tremendous reception" and that Nokia would be in a
position to show "strong profitability" on mobile phones after
its costs cutting measures.
He also said the group's second quarter profit -- up 82
percent on Q1 to 728 million markka -- was a very clear
indication of which way the trend was going.
Much of analysts' optimism was based on the upbeat CEO
comments and they said there was no reason to expect any
significant surprises since the company has not issued a
profit-warning.
Any upset in the interim -- particularly on the mobile
phones side -- could therefore deal a major blow to management
credibility with serious shockwaves on the stockmarket, some
said.
FIM Pankkiiriliike analyst Niklas Geust said he assumed that
Nokia's Q1 loss in mobile phones was bigger than the unit's
profit in Q2 since otherwise the company would have said mobile
phones had a first-half profit.
But by now that loss should have been erased, he said.
"They should have made a clear profit," he said adding that
he would consider 200 million markka enough at a quarterly level
at this stage.
Handelsbanken's Andersson said the price erosion in mobile
handsets had been dampened by consumers' willingness to pay a
quality premium for products like Nokia's and Ericsson's.
"I think price elasticity has been smaller than expected at
these price levels," he said.
In 1995 -- Nokia's best year ever -- the mobile phones unit
posted a 1.75 billion markka operating profit, 11 percent of net
sales, and the telecommunications arm posted a 2.72 billion
profit, 26.3 percent of net sales.
If Nokia lives up to the expectation that its handset
worries are behind -- and that the infrastructure business is
more or less as strong as it has been -- the outlook for next
year is good, analysts said.
Normal consolidated quarterly profits for Nokia should be
well above one billion markka, they said, and their forecasts
for next year are for a record profit before taxes of around six
billion markka.
The U.S. market, which is entering the digital era, offers
opportunities in 1997, and unlike previous estimates, not many
more competitors would be able to enter the market, they said.
Poul Ernest Jessen at Den Danske Bank said Ericsson's large
handset order from AT&T and its advances in China had changed
his view on when new competition will emerge.
"It is a new situation, operators want to make sure they get
the phones they need ... and it gives the large players an
advantage in large scale production," Jessen said.
FORECAST DETAILS
A Reuters survey of analysts covering Finnish equities
showed a 2.2 billion markka median forecast for
telecommunications group Nokia Oy's January-September profit
before tax and minorities.
Profit before tax and minorities EPS*
(FIM million) (FIM)
Median 2,198 5.5
Lowest 2,010 4.8
Highest 2,427 6.1
*EPS forecasts by 11 analysts of 19 in the survey.
Nokia's nine-month results are due for release on November
14 around 1200/1000 GMT.
In January-September 1995, Nokia posted a 3.98 billion
markka proforma profit before tax and minorities.
The analysts polled by Reuters forecast for Nokia a
full-year 1996 median profit of 3.75 billion markka (range
3.20-4.09 billion markka), and a median EPS of 9.4 markka (range
7.7-10.6 markka). (Full-year 1996 profit forecasts by 18 of the
19 respondents, full-year EPS forecasts by 16).
Nokia's 1995 profit before tax and minorities was 4.93
billion markka.
Contributors to the survey were AG Securities, Aros, Alfred
Berg, BZW Securities, Carnegie, Danske Bank, Enskilda, Erik
Selin, Evli Securities, FSB Securities, FIM Securities,
Handelsbanken, Interbank, Merita, Morgan Stanley, Opstock,
Paribas, Postipankki and Warburg Securities.
